thread.title: Fanuc Still Strong In Robots And Automation, But Trouble May Lie Ahead - Fanuc Corporation ADR (OTCMKTS:FANUY)

author: Stephen Simpson, CFA
title: Fanuc Still Strong In Robots And Automation, But Trouble May Lie Ahead - Fanuc Corporation ADR (OTCMKTS:FANUY)
text:
I’ve never been quite as fond of Japan’s Fanuc ( OTCPK:FANUY ) (6954.T) as many readers seem to be, and over the last five years you could have done better with other automation names like Yaskawa ( OTCPK:YASKY ), Rockwell ( ROK ), Keyence ( OTCPK:KYCCF ), or HollySys ( HOLI ) (though the two-year comps are more forgiving to Fanuc). While Fanuc has done better than I’d expected over the last two years in terms of revenue growth, leveraging a strong rebound in machine tool and robomachinery orders, margins and FCF generation haven’t been all that impressive as business has skewed to lower-margin products.
Now there are macro clouds on the horizon. Weaker smartphone capex demands seem likely to pressure results in 2018 and we may be nearing the point of peak machine tool orders, setting the stage for what could be a nasty decline over the next few years. I do expect Fanuc to continue to see strong growth in robots and robotic components, but I’m just not excited about the valuation today given those challenges and potential risks.
Is The Machine Tool Cycle Coming To An End? Japanese machine tool cycles have typically run about 18 months, with larger “super-cycles” that typically extend out to about 10 – 15 years. The current up-cycle is at 18 months (and close to the 10-year mark from the last trough), and while May’s machine tool orders in Japan were still up 15%, the 18 th -straight year-over-year improvement, orders have started shrinking on a month-to-month basis and orders from outside Japan have slowed significantly (up 10% in the month of May).
There are a lot of moving parts with the machine tool industry, but auto OEMs have typically been among the biggest customers. While there is still strength in some parts of the auto sector (Keyence and Cognex ( CGNX ) have been seeing good machine vision orders), overall auto capex has been slowing noticeably. Coupled with signs of weakness in many other industrial sectors, that’s potentially bad news for Fanuc and its FA Systems business. I’d also note that when those super-cycles peak out, orders can plunge by as much as two-thirds in just two years.
Perhaps this decline won’t be as severe, or maybe there’s more life in the cycle than recent numbers suggest. Even so, I’d note that Fanuc has been losing some share in its core CNC business (the “brains” of machine tools) and facing more competition in its servo business from companies like THK ( OTCPK:THKLY ).
Smartphones Taking Their Toll Fanuc has sizable business exposure to smartphone capex, and particularly the Apple ( AAPL ) production/supply chain. In the past, this business has followed a “one great year, two weak year” patterns, and it looks like 2018 is going to be a tough year after strong orders and revenue in 2017. To give some sense of the exposure, around half of the Robomachinery business is tied to smartphones, about 15% of the FA Systems business, and about 5% to 10% of the Robots business – all told, making up about 20% of Fanuc’s revenue.
Fanuc’s main competitor in robodrills, Brother , offered pretty grim guidance for its business in early May, pointing to a 20% revenue drop in the 2019 fiscal year (which ends in March 2019, so covering much of 2018). For its part, Fanuc is already seeing significant declines as well – Goldman Sachs analyst Yuichiro Isayama tracks customs data to try to get a sense of Fanuc’s shipping trends, and it looks like Robodrill shipments were down more than 50% in the month of May. While Apple’s discussion of its capex plans (likely in early November) could help resolve some of the worries that have hit many players in the automation space, particularly Japanese companies, that’s still a long wait for what may or may not be good news.
Robots Still A Strong Opportunity Fanuc remains the leading player in robots, though ABB ( ABB ), Yaskawa, and KUKA ( OTCPK:KUKAY ) are serious, focused competitors in their own right. Although growth has slowed over the last three quarters, in keeping with the idea that auto OEMs are spending less on capex (auto is about 50% of the business here), the business still grew 13% yoy in Fanuc’s last quarter, and order growth remains in the mid-teens, with a book-to-bill above 1.
As the global leader in robots, I believe Fanuc is well-positioned for the ongoing expansion of robots outside of traditional strongholds like auto assembly. I do have some concerns, though, about the pace of innovation here. While Fanuc does indeed make very high-quality robots, the company doesn’t seem to be making the same investments into new markets like Yaskawa (service robots), ABB (cobots), or KUKA (aerospace assembly). This may well be only a product of self-promotion, but I do also believe that Fanuc has some vulnerability to the growing acceptance of cheaper domestically-made robots in markets like China.
The Opportunity I’m not really worried about Fanuc’s long-term future, and I believe the company can generate revenue growth in the mid-single-digits. The next couple of years could be dicey, though, depending upon what happens with smartphone, auto, and general industrial capex spending. I’m also not too worried about the long-term outlook for margins and FCF. While recent years have been pressured by a sudden surge in lower-margin business orders and management’s decision to reinvest in the business, I expect long-term FCF generation to be strong. That said, once again the shorter-term outlook is cloudier – Fanuc operates with relatively high fixed costs, and a significant near-term slowdown in margins will hit operating margins.
The Bottom Line Fanuc shares don’t look undervalued to me on the basis of discounted cash flow, but that’s the norm today across the automation space and Fanuc doesn’t look meaningfully more expensive than Keyence or Yaskawa by that metric. There does appear to be some modest upside by way of EV/EBITDA, but not enough to tempt me given the potential near-term end-market headwinds. While I know Fanuc is a well-loved name in the space (a position it has earned over the years) and I’m sure many readers will affirm their long-term support for the shares, I’m not interested at today’s risk/benefit trade-off.
Disclosure: I am/we are long ABB.
